'''''Brachychiton populneus''''', commonly known as the '''kurrajong''',<ref>Floyd, A.G., ''Rainforest Trees of Mainland South-eastern Australia'', 1989, p391</ref> is a small to medium-sized [[tree]] found naturally in [[Australia]] in a diversity of habitats from wetter coastal districts to [[semi-arid]] interiors of [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], [[New South Wales]] and [[Queensland]]. ''Carrejun'' and ''carrejan'' were the indigenous names of trees in the foothills of the [[Blue Mountains (New South Wales)|Blue Mountains]] near Sydney, and the bark was used for twine and fishing lines.<ref>Sarskens G. ''People of the River '', 2020, p180</ref>

==Description==
The tree is drought-tolerant and the extended trunk is a water storage device for survival in a warm, dry climate. The bell-shaped flowers vary in colour from pale cream to pink, while the leaves vary considerably in shape. The leaves are either simple and pointed, or may be 3–9 lobed. Saplings grow from a drought and fire-resistant tap-rooted [[tuber]].

At present, there are two noted subspecies of ''Brachychiton populneus''.<ref>{{cite web | title=Brachychiton populneus - Growing Native Plants | url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2002/brachychiton-populneus.html | access-date=2025-05-06 | archive-date=2026-05-15 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260515132406/https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2002/brachychiton-populneus.html | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Brachychiton populneus | Australian Plants Society | date=9 August 2023 | url=https://resources.austplants.com.au/plant/brachychiton-populneuskurrajong/ | access-date=6 May 2025 | archive-date=6 May 2025 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250506153150/https://resources.austplants.com.au/plant/brachychiton-populneuskurrajong/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

These are:

• ''Brachychiton populneus'' subsp. ''populneus'' 

• ''Brachychiton populneus'' subsp. ''trilobus''

==Uses==
The kurrajong has multiple uses and was used by many [[Aboriginal Australians|Australian Aboriginal]] clans and tribes around Australia. As [[Bush tucker|bush food]] or "bush tucker", the seeds located in a seed pod were often removed, cleaned of the irritating fine hairs within the seed pod, and roasted for eating.<ref name=low88>{{cite book | author=Low, Tim |title=Wild Food Plants of Australia |isbn= 0-207-14383-8 | page=183 |publisher=Angus & Robertson | year= 1988}}</ref> Water could be obtained from the tree roots by boring a hole in the trunk and squeezing the wood.<ref>Ngarigo Plant Use in the Snowy River Catchment</ref> There are also records of the seed pods being turned into a children's rattle or toy. The soft, spongy wood was used for making shields, and the bark as a fibre. The leaves are also used as emergency fodder for drought-affected animal stock. There are records of European settlers using the seeds as a coffee supplement by roasting and crushing the seeds.<ref name=low88/>

==Adaptation==
It has been introduced as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental tree]] to south-western Australia, [[South Africa]], [[Louisiana]], [[California]], [[Arizona]] and [[Mediterranean Basin|Mediterranean]] countries. In [[Western Australia]] it was observed to be [[Invasive species|invasive]] in disturbed areas.

==Hybrids==
Horticulturists have hybridised the kurrajong with related ''[[Brachychiton]]'' species, including the Queensland bottle tree (''[[Brachychiton rupestris|B. rupestris]]'') and Illawarra flame tree (''[[Brachychiton acerifolius|B. acerifolius]]'') to produce new garden [[Ornamental plant|ornamentals]].{{cn|date=March 2022}}

==Name==
The specific name ''populneus'' pertains to a perceived similarity to the ''[[Populus]]'' genus, i.e. the poplars. Sometimes ''B. populneus'' is also known by the names "lacebark kurrajong" and "bottle tree" (USA). However, ''[[Brachychiton discolor|B. discolor]]'' is also referred to as the lacebark kurrajong, and bottle tree is a term commonly applied not only to other species of ''[[Brachychiton]]'' but to members of other ''genera'' around the world. The kurrajong has been recorded as a host plant for the mistletoe species ''[[Dendrophthoe glabrescens]]'' a [[Parasitic plant|hemi-parasite]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Downey |first=Paul O. |year=1998 |title=An inventory of host species for each aerial mistletoe species (Loranthaceae and Viscaceae) in Australia |journal=Cunninghamia |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=685–720 |url=http://rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0018/58041/Cun5Dow685.pdf |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426091532/http://rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0018/58041/Cun5Dow685.pdf |archivedate=2012-04-26 }}</ref>
